# Session 7: Prompt Design — Zero-shot vs Few-shot

## 📋 Agenda

- The **anatomy** of a prompt — four elements
- **Zero-shot vs. few-shot**, and **chain-of-thought**
- The wider **design space** — what to *run* vs. what to *know about*
- Two traps: **contamination** and the **validation/test split**

Our worked example all session: **Huang & Mizumoto (2025)** — writing-feedback prompts.

## 🎯 Learning Objectives

By the end of this session, you will be able to:

- **Name the four prompt elements** — *instruction · context · input data · output indicator* — and locate each in a real prompt.
- Distinguish **zero-shot** from **few-shot** prompting and judge **when examples help**.
- Explain **chain-of-thought** and where it earns its keep.
- Place a technique on the **run-it-this-week vs. know-it-exists** line.
- Explain the **train/test contamination** trap and why you **tune on validation, report on test**.

::: {.callout-note}
The message of the day: *prompting is a **design space**, not a single trick — small structural choices move the score.*
:::

# The anatomy of a prompt

## Prompting *is* a design space

An LLM does what the **prompt** tells it to. Change the prompt, change the output — and the score.

. . .

So a prompt is not a magic phrase you either know or don't. It has **parts you can design deliberately** — and today we learn those parts on one concrete example.

## Four elements of a prompt {.smaller}

Chen et al. (2023), via **Huang & Mizumoto (2025)** — an effective prompt typically has four parts:

- **Instruction** — what the model should *do* (start with a verb: *classify, summarize, explain*).
- **Context** — the background, role, rubric, or level that scopes the task.
- **Input data** — the actual text to be processed.
- **Output indicator** — the *form* of the answer (format, tone, "only feedback, no rewrite").

. . .

If one of the four is missing, the output usually misses too.

## The running example — writing feedback {.smaller}

**Huang & Mizumoto's Example Prompt 2** — a structured paragraph-feedback prompt for an EFL class:

> **Task** — Based on the following criteria, review the following paragraph and provide specific feedback… **I am not seeking rewrite, give me only feedback.**
>
> **Criteria** — 1. Hook / Attention-grabber · 2. Background / Context · 3. Thesis statement · 4. Organization · 5. Clarity & coherence
>
> **My paragraph** — *(paste your paragraph here)*

. . .

Read the four elements straight off it:

| Element | In this prompt |
|---|---|
| **Instruction** | "review… and provide specific feedback" |
| **Context** | the 5-item **Criteria** rubric |
| **Input data** | "My paragraph" |
| **Output indicator** | "only feedback, no rewrite" |

# Zero-shot, few-shot, chain-of-thought

## Zero-shot vs. few-shot {.smaller}

- **Zero-shot** — instruction only, **no examples**. The model relies on what it already knows. Great for simple, familiar tasks.
- **Few-shot** — you include **a few worked examples** *(input → correct label)* right in the prompt, so the model infers the pattern.

. . .

**When do examples help?** When the task is specialized, the label set is your own, or the format must be exact. Two tips (promptingguide.ai):

- keep a **consistent format** across all examples;
- make the examples' **label space representative** — don't show only one class.

## Chain-of-thought (CoT) {.smaller}

Ask the model to **reason in steps** before answering (Wei et al., 2022).

**Huang & Mizumoto's Example Prompt 1** is CoT feedback:

> *First,* read the paragraph to understand its main idea. *Next,* check the structure… *Then,* identify grammatical errors. *After that,* assess clarity and coherence. **Provide feedback based on these steps.**

. . .

Zero-shot CoT is often just one added line — **"Let's think step by step"** (Kojima et al., 2022).

::: {.callout-tip}
CoT earns its keep on tasks that need **sequential judgement** — reviewing writing, or deciding a borderline label.
:::

## Iterating a prompt: Ex 1 → Ex 2 {.smaller}

The *same* feedback task, tightened:

- **Ex 1 (generic)** — "give feedback on this paragraph, step by step." Works, but vague.
- **Ex 2 (structured)** — split into **Task / Criteria / My paragraph**, add the output indicator "only feedback."

. . .

That move — generic → structured — is **prompt iteration**. You'll do the data-driven version of it in **S9**, reading the errors and tightening the *Criteria*.

# The wider design space

## Run it this week vs. know it exists {.smaller}

| **Run it in S8** | **Know it exists** (name & reason, don't run) |
|---|---|
| zero-shot | **self-consistency** — sample N, majority-vote (a reproducibility lever → S10) |
| few-shot | **RAG** — ground the model on the annotation manual / codebook (≈ *dynamic* few-shot) |
| chain-of-thought | **agentic / multi-step** — the model plans → critiques its own label → revises |
| structured output | (ReAct, Reflexion, prompt chaining…) |

. . .

Your self-study map for all of these: **[promptingguide.ai/techniques](https://www.promptingguide.ai/techniques)**.

## Two traps before you tune {.smaller}

- **Train/test contamination** — never draw your **few-shot examples from the gold set** you score on. The model would be "shown the answers."
- **Validation vs. test** — **tune** the prompt on a small **validation** set; **report** the final number **once** on a held-out **test** set.

. . .

Both protect the one thing an evaluation is for: **an honest estimate of how the prompt does on unseen text.**
